narrative:
The model predicts you have a 15% chance of failing your final year, which is low enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution to protect your chances of graduating.

The three factors that most strongly influenced this decision were your reason for choosing the school, your clean record of past failures, and the quality of your family relationships. Surprisingly, these elements pushed the prediction in different directions. Your choice of the school based on its strong reputation was the most powerful factor and worked in your favor, pulling the outcome toward passing because students who pick this school for its reputation tend to do better. Your zero past class failures was the second most important element and also supported a passing outcome, as having no previous failures is typical of students who ultimately succeed.

However, the quality of your family relationships emerged as the third strongest influence and worked against you. Even though you described your family relationships as good, this feature still nudged the model toward predicting failure. This suggests that, compared with other students who passed, something in how family dynamics interact with your other circumstances is not providing the same protective effect.

To improve, focus on strengthening the supportive elements already working for you. Since you want to pursue higher education and have no history of failures, consider increasing your weekly study time beyond the 2–5 hours you currently spend and making fuller use of family support to create stronger accountability at home. These small, consistent changes can help turn your 15% risk into a much safer path to passing. (248 words)
